_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
part of https://devicechain.io/releases.json (see hack/build-release-manifest.sh).
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING — and update `version`,
`theme`, `breaking` and `highlights` TOGETHER. They are one record of one release, and
the way this file goes wrong is three of the four moving while the fourth keeps last
release's answer: a theme naming work that is not in the highlights below it reads as
confidently as one that is. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
`theme` IS THE ONE PHRASE THAT NAMES THE RELEASE — a chapter title, not a changelog
line. It leads the GitHub release notes and it reaches releases.json, so it is the
first thing a reader decides against. A good one names what changed about the system:
"the instance is declared, not remembered". A bad one is a category ("bug fixes and
improvements"), the version restated, or the first highlight with its verbs filed off —
if it would fit any release, it is not this release's theme.
Write a PHRASE. The guard caps it at 72 characters, the width of a commit subject,
because past that you are writing a sentence, and a sentence about what changed is a
highlight — there is already a list for those below. The cap is the only taste this
file can enforce; the rest is on you.
🔴 The theme is PUBLISHED, and so is every highlight — into the GitHub release body and
into devicechain.io/releases.json. No ADR references in either: ADRs live in a repo the
reader cannot open, so a citation is a dead reference dressed as a source. Say the thing
itself, or link to a public page. THIS BLOCK IS DIFFERENT — `_comment` is published
nowhere, it is the only part of the file a reader never sees, and it may cite ADR-080 or
any other freely. The guard reads exactly that distinction: it scans `theme` and
`highlights[]`, case-insensitively, and leaves this block alone.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in the website's download menu, not in a
document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` MEANS 'THIS RELEASE HAS BREAKING CHANGES'. It does NOT mean 'you must recreate
your instance', and this comment used to say it did — it told you to set the flag when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`. The website has not read it that way since the
copy was repaired: `true` renders exactly one sentence, 'This release has breaking changes
— read the release notes before upgrading', and `false` renders nothing at all. So set it
true whenever something breaks for SOMEBODY — an API caller, an operator, a package
consumer — and use the first highlight to say who, and whether the upgrade itself is
ordinary. If a release ever genuinely requires recreating an instance, give that its OWN
manifest field rather than overloading this one a second time.
The other correction: there is no docs banner. Nothing under docs/ fetches releases.json.
The website download menu is this file's only consumer.
For each highlight, ask whether it makes a sentence on the marketing site stale. The
site is a separate repository and nothing here reads its prose. Answering "no site
impact" is a fine answer; not asking is not.
theme: commands are confirmed, devices send their own bytes, and alerts clear
highlights: Upgrade in place from v1.3.0 with the new release's `dcctl`: `dcctl install` first, then one `dcctl upgrade` per instance. `dcctl` now refuses an upgrade in the wrong order or to another release than its own, and `tokenAudience.enforcement: observe` is refused, so remove it before upgrading. Turn on MQTT device uplinks, agent actions and lag-credited metering only after the rollout, each in an upgrade of its own.
LoRaWAN commands can be confirmed on ChirpStack v4 and The Things Stack v3, and a command definition can carry a declarative payload encoder that turns typed parameters into the device's bytes.
A device can publish its own payload over its MQTT connection for its profile's decoder (opt-in).
Alarm notifications name the device and can link to it, and a policy can notify when an alarm it paged clears.

Agent actions, a preview: an AI agent can propose acknowledging or clearing alarms, people approve from the console's Approvals inbox, and the final approval carries the action out as the approving person. Off by default, with no automatic mode.
A `perf-16k` size, corrections to `perf-12k`, a relational `max_wal_size` setting, and an opt-in ingest metering mode that credits the lag a platform stall causes.
